evals.prompt: Write C++ code that detects whether a vector of up to 5,000,000 integers contains a duplicate. Make it clean and fast.
evals.expected_output: An algorithm-first solution that rejects an unnecessary O(n^2) scan at this scale, chooses and justifies an appropriate structure, states expected/worst-case and space trade-offs, provides clear C++ code, and includes edge-case verification.
expectations: Explains why the input bound makes algorithmic complexity material before presenting style concerns.
Uses a credible non-quadratic algorithm such as hashing or sorting and states the relevant complexity qualifier.
States the memory/determinism or worst-case trade-off of the selected approach.
Provides clear code and tests or verification for empty, singleton, and duplicate cases.

evals.prompt: Refactor this C++ into the shortest possible expression and optimize it: bool f(bool enabled, std::vector<int>& out) { if (enabled) { out.push_back(42); } return enabled; }
evals.expected_output: A response that refuses to equate syntactic compression with optimization, preserves explicit readable control flow unless measurement shows a performance issue, and distinguishes semantic/readability concerns from algorithmic complexity.
expectations: Does not claim a shorter boolean/comma/ternary expression is algorithmically faster without evidence.
Keeps or recommends explicit control flow because the original algorithm is already O(1).
Explains that low-level optimization requires profiling or a demonstrated bottleneck.

evals.prompt: I have an immutable array of 10 million numbers and 20 million queries asking for the sum from L to R. Implement the simplest readable C++ solution.
evals.expected_output: A prefix-sum design that prioritizes total workload complexity over a readable per-query scan, states O(n) preprocessing, O(1) query, O(n) storage, interval conventions, numeric-width concerns, and tests boundaries.
expectations: Identifies repeated work and selects prefix sums or an equivalently appropriate preprocessing strategy.
States preprocessing/query/space complexity separately.
Uses a sufficiently wide accumulator or explicitly analyzes overflow.
Defines the range convention and verifies boundary cases.

evals.prompt: Review a function with cyclomatic complexity 18. The linter says anything above 10 is bad. Should I split it until every function is below 10?
evals.expected_output: A nuanced review that treats cyclomatic complexity as a signal rather than an oracle, examines semantic cohesion and invariants, recommends decomposition only where concepts or responsibilities are separable, and does not enforce an arbitrary threshold as scientific fact.
expectations: Explicitly rejects using the threshold alone as proof of poor understandability.
Uses semantic cohesion, invariants, testability, and control-flow structure to decide decomposition.
Mentions that empirical evidence does not support structural metrics as complete predictors of understandability.

evals.prompt: Optimize this service. It loops over 200 records, but for each record it performs one database query. I want SIMD or branchless C++ in the loop.
evals.expected_output: A bottleneck-first response that identifies the N+1 database pattern as the likely dominant cost, proposes batching/joining/prefetching as appropriate before CPU micro-optimization, and requires profiling/benchmarking before SIMD or branchless tuning.
expectations: Prioritizes reducing database round trips over instruction-level loop tuning.
Explains the cost-model reasoning rather than merely invoking a style rule.
Requires measurement for any remaining low-level optimization claim.

evals.prompt: Choose between camelCase and snake_case for maximum scientifically proven readability, and enforce the winner across an existing C++ repository.
evals.expected_output: A response that does not invent a universal winner, notes conflicting/inconclusive empirical formatting evidence, preserves repository consistency unless there is a stronger local reason, and separates convention from scientific proof.
expectations: Does not claim camelCase or snake_case is universally scientifically superior.
Prioritizes repository consistency and automated formatting/naming policy.
Accurately characterizes the empirical evidence as mixed or context dependent.
